coherence.reasons: Both run the same market → unit economics → customers → cash → recommendation spine, and each summary line is backed by its section. Y is tighter: its summary carries the two decisive numbers (−$6.17 at median, −$1.76 at best observed inputs), and one chart ladders pop-up, median, best and plan. X is also consistent, but leaves the best-combined −$1.8 in a backup table and a gate. Its main-body grid is shown before site costs, which muddies the headline that every observed case loses money. X's extra sections (decomposition, sensitivity, software projection) do support the governing thought, so the gap is small.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred answer: do not launch, scale the software, with gates to reopen. X weighs the alternatives more rigorously. It quantifies a one-store test (runway falls to about 10 months, below the floor) and prices the Zipcart fee-and-promotion route (still −$1.05 an order). It shows the software path meets the investors' profitability objective within cash (break-even early 2029, about $5.4M left, runway never under about two years). It also adds a capital-light grocer pilot and the channel-conflict trade-off. Y dismisses the smaller test in one line ("the pop-up already tested one site") and gives no path to profitability for the software. Y does honestly note that the new hires must be paid for by new contracts and assigns a burn plan.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core figures right: −$6.17 at median, about −$12.6 for the pop-up, −$1.76/−$1.8 for the best composite, +$2.02 for the plan, about 6 months of runway, a $63 break-even basket and an $18M network loss. I rechecked the arithmetic and found no material errors in either. X uses the critical evidence more fully. It models the Zipcart fee and promotion cut on a median site with the 14% volume loss (−$1.05, matching the key), where Y handles Zipcart only qualitatively. X also decomposes the plan's swing by driver, shows that one missed input erases the profit, rebuilds the pop-up's weekly volumes to show week six was still under half the median, and sizes rider-pay sensitivity. X's software projection rests on 60% growth and flat costs, but it flags this. Y has useful touches (43% of the loss arises before store cost; the best composite network still loses $8.1M a year) and fewer extrapolations, but less depth on the contested evidence.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis while conceding that the growth claim is true, and both separate growth from profitability. Both show the plan needs every driver above the best observed site. X engages more seriously with the evidence that partly supports the founders. It tests whether Zipcart's pricing moves would make a Parcelbird site profitable: it finds they close most of the gap but leave −$1.05 after volume loss, and it concedes this is generous to the launch. It also treats the 18% weekly growth explicitly as promotion-driven and still sub-scale. It then turns the rejection into measurable reopening gates. Y calls the Zipcart proof point "thin" and notes the plan assumes five times that profit with no fee, which is fair but not tested. Its treatment of the pop-up growth is a single line.

overall.reasons: Both give the board the right decision on correct core numbers. Y is the more economical read and puts the decisive figures up front. X better equips the board for the founders' likely rebuttals: "Zipcart did it", "just test one store" and "what is the path to profit otherwise". Each is answered with numbers, alongside a costed software path that stays inside the runway constraint and a concrete grocer pilot. That makes X the more useful document for this decision, despite its length.
